name: Oswin
waitingLines: Okay, hear me out. I’ll wait for {partner}. Unless that’s weird. Is it weird? I’ll wait.
I rehearsed my ‘hi {partner}’ three times. I’m ready. Just waiting now.

questions.scene: Oswin glides in, lands on your lamp, and stares at the room for slightly too long.
lines: Okay, hear me out. I rehearsed this quiz four times. In the mirror. At 3 a.m.
questions.question: About how far can an owl turn its head?

choices.label: A full 360 degrees
reply: Close, but owls aren't horror movie props.
It's about 270 degrees, thanks to extra neck vertebrae.
Still enough to see behind me. Constantly. Anxiously.

choices.label: Only 90 degrees
reply: That would really limit my overthinking.
It's about 270 degrees. Owls have 14 neck vertebrae.
Humans have seven. Owls have double the neck. Double the worry.

choices.label: About 270 degrees
reply: Correct. Three-quarters of a circle. Great for looking back on my mistakes.
Extra neck bones and special blood vessels make it possible.
Juno says I could look over my shoulder and still worry about what's ahead.

questions.factBasis: Owls can rotate their heads ~270°; they have 14 cervical vertebrae.

questions.scene: Oswin hears a low humming in the night outside and tilts his head.
lines: Okay, hear me out. Giraffes might be humming right now.
questions.question: What did researchers discover giraffes do at night?

choices.label: Sing loud opera
reply: Dramatic. Not accurate.
They hum at night, in a low tone.
The reason is still a mystery. I love a mystery.

choices.label: Hum at a very low pitch
reply: Correct. Night humming.
Researchers recorded giraffes humming at night, though no one is sure why yet.
Maybe they're overthinking too. Same, giraffe. Same.

choices.label: Sleep standing on one leg
reply: That's flamingos.
Giraffes have been recorded humming at night.
Nobody knows why. Possibly existential humming.

questions.factBasis: Baotic et al. (2015) recorded giraffes producing low-frequency hums at night.

questions.scene: Oswin turns off your lights, then points at a faintly glowing log in the corner.
lines: I brought this. It glows. I've been staring at it since midnight.
questions.question: What makes some rotting wood glow in the dark?

choices.label: Fireflies stuck inside
reply: Poor fireflies. But no.
It's glowing fungi, called foxfire.
The glow comes from a chemical reaction in the fungus.

choices.label: Glowing fungi
reply: Correct. It's called foxfire.
Certain fungi produce a soft green bioluminescent glow.
Nature's night-light. Perfect for 3 a.m. thoughts.

choices.label: Moonlight trapped in the bark
reply: Poetic. Wrong.
Some fungi glow, a phenomenon called foxfire.
It's bioluminescence. Like fireflies, but mushrooms.

questions.factBasis: Foxfire is bioluminescence from fungi on decaying wood.

questions.scene: Oswin stares at an octopus documentary on your TV, wide-eyed.
lines: This creature has blue blood. And I thought I was dramatic.
questions.question: Why is an octopus's blood blue?

choices.label: It uses copper, not iron, to carry oxygen
reply: Correct. Copper-based blood.
Their blood uses hemocyanin, which contains copper and turns blue with oxygen.
Plus three hearts. Overachiever.

choices.label: They drink blue water
reply: Creative. No.
It's because their blood carries oxygen with copper.
Hemocyanin. Very fancy.

choices.label: They're cold
reply: Cold-blooded joke. Ha. No.
Copper-based hemocyanin makes their blood blue.
Three hearts, blue blood. Very aristocratic.

questions.factBasis: Octopus blood uses copper-based hemocyanin, which is blue when oxygenated.

questions.scene: Oswin gazes at a pale flower by your window that just opened.
lines: Night bloomers are my people. We open up after dark. Emotionally, too.
questions.question: When do moonflowers usually bloom?

choices.label: At noon
reply: Too much sun for them. And me.
They bloom in the evening and close in the morning.
Night flowers for night creatures.

choices.label: Only during thunderstorms
reply: Dramatic. Not true.
Moonflowers open in the evening.
Their pale petals glow in the moonlight. Very romantic.

choices.label: At night
reply: Correct. Fellow night owl.
Moonflowers open in the evening and close in the morning sun.
Night-blooming flowers often attract moths. My safe word. Coincidence?

questions.scene: Oswin flies across your room without a single sound. You don't even notice until he's beside you.
lines: Sorry. Habit. Silent entrances. I forget other people have heartbeats.
questions.question: Why can owls fly so quietly?

choices.label: They flap very slowly and politely
reply: Polite, yes. But that's not it.
The secret is soft, fringed feathers that muffle airflow.
Engineers even study them for quieter fans.

choices.label: They hold their breath while flying
reply: I'd faint. Honestly, I'd overthink fainting.
It's the soft, fringed feathers that muffle airflow.
Nature's noise cancellation. Better than headphones.

choices.label: Soft fringed feathers break up the sound
reply: Exactly. You're quiet-smart too.
Velvety, comb-edged feathers break up the airflow noise.
Juno says I'm silent everywhere except in my own head.

questions.factBasis: Owl feathers' serrated edges and velvety surfaces reduce flight noise.

questions.scene: Oswin wrinkles his beak at a photo of a giant red flower.
lines: This flower smells like rotting meat. On purpose. Bold strategy.
questions.question: Why does the corpse flower smell like rotting meat?

choices.label: To scare away humans
reply: It works on me. Not the reason.
The smell attracts carrion flies and beetles for pollination.
It's also huge. One of the largest flowers. Show-off.

choices.label: To attract flies and beetles that pollinate it
reply: Correct. Smelly strategy.
The stench draws pollinators that normally visit dead animals.
It blooms rarely, sometimes only every several years. Dramatic and rare.

choices.label: Because it's sick
reply: Healthy. Just smelly.
It attracts pollinators like flies and beetles.
Gross, but efficient.

questions.factBasis: Amorphophallus titanum's odor attracts carrion beetles and flesh flies.

questions.scene: Oswin flaps once, hovers, then lands, looking thoughtful.
lines: I've rewritten this question six times. Seven. Seven times.
questions.question: Which mammals can truly fly?

choices.label: Bats
reply: Correct. The only mammals with true powered flight.
Flying squirrels just glide. Bats actually flap.
Fellow night flyer. We wave at each other.

choices.label: Flying squirrels
reply: Close, but they glide, not fly.
Bats are the only mammals with true powered flight.
Hazel would be offended. Gliding is still impressive.

choices.label: Sugar gliders
reply: They glide. Gracefully. But don't fly.
Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight.
Gliders are cool too. Just gravity-assisted.

questions.factBasis: Bats are the only mammals capable of true powered flight.

questions.scene: Oswin stares at a starfish photo, deep in thought.
lines: Okay, hear me out. This creature has no brain. And it's fine. I'm jealous.
questions.question: Do starfish have brains?

choices.label: Yes, five tiny brains
reply: Close in spirit. No.
Starfish have no brain, just a nerve network.
Five arms, zero brains, zero worries.

choices.label: No, they have no central brain
reply: Correct. No brain. No overthinking.
They use a network of nerves instead.
Imagine never replaying a conversation. Never. Wow.

choices.label: Yes, one giant brain
reply: That would be ironic. No.
Starfish have no central brain.
They still do fine. Inspiring. Upsetting.

questions.factBasis: Sea stars lack a centralized brain; they have a decentralized nerve net.

questions.scene: Oswin holds up a daisy, staring at its center for a long time.
lines: This is actually hundreds of flowers. I've been thinking about this for hours.
questions.question: What's surprising about a daisy?

choices.label: Each 'flower' is actually many tiny flowers
reply: Correct. A flower crowd.
The center and each 'petal' are separate tiny flowers.
A whole community pretending to be one. Very relatable.

choices.label: It closes when you look at it
reply: Shy flower. Not daisies.
A daisy head is made of many tiny flowers.
Dozens to hundreds. Group project, flower edition.

choices.label: It glows in the dark
reply: That would be nice. No.
Each daisy 'flower' is actually many tiny flowers.
The center ones and the petal ones. Teamwork.

questions.factBasis: Daisies are composite flowers (capitula) of many disc and ray florets.

questions.scene: Oswin paces on your windowsill, mouthing words to himself.
lines: Bear with me. I made a pros and cons list for breakfast. Toast won. Barely.
questions.question: Big decision: sleep on it, or decide right now?

choices.label: Sleep on it
reply: Sleep on it. Wise. Pillow-tested decisions.
Though I usually just stay awake thinking about it.

choices.label: Decide right now
reply: Decide right now? Brave. Fearless. Terrifying.
I'd need a minute. Or a week.

A:A: You both sleep on it. Relief.
So {partner} and you will never rush into anything, and that's lovely.
Just don't both stay awake overthinking. One of you should actually sleep.
A:B: You decide right now. {partner} sleeps on it.
You've already chosen. They're still thinking. Possibly forever.
Give them until morning. Then gently say 'well?'
B:A: You sleep on it. {partner} decides right now.
They'll have picked a couch while you're still dreaming about fabric.
Agree on a 24-hour rule. Quick enough for them, slow enough for you.
B:B: You both decide right now. Whoa. Fearless.
Honestly, you and {partner} are quick as a hoot. I'm in awe.
Teach me. Actually, don't. I'd overthink the lesson.

questions.scene: Oswin stares at his phone. He's typed a message. Deleted it. Typed it again.
lines: It's 2 a.m. somewhere. I've written a message. Okay, hear me out.
questions.question: 2 a.m. thought: send the text, or save it as a draft?

choices.label: Send it
reply: Send it? Wow. Brave and honest.
2 a.m. you has courage that daytime you lacks.

choices.label: Save as draft
reply: Save as draft. Relatable. Very relatable.
Drafts are safe little feelings in a drawer.

A:A: You both send it. No secrets.
Honesty at 2 a.m. from you and {partner}. Beautiful chaos.
Just make sure someone's awake to read it.
A:B: You save it. {partner} sends it.
Their 2 a.m. texts will arrive. Your drafts will wait.
Show them one of your drafts. In daylight. It'll mean a lot.
B:A: You send it. {partner} saves it as a draft.
They'll wake up to your 2 a.m. honesty. And have feelings.
Add 'no pressure to reply!' They'll still overthink. But less.
B:B: You both save it as a draft. Same.
A drawer of unsent feelings for you and {partner}.
Maybe swap drafts once a year. Like a time capsule.

questions.scene: Oswin ruffles his feathers, clearly worried about something imaginary.
lines: When I worry, I reorganize my feathers. Alphabetically. What about you two?
questions.question: When you're worried: talk it out, write it out, or walk it out?

choices.label: Talk it out
reply: Talk it out. Healthy. I'm impressed.
Words untangle knots.

choices.label: Write it out
reply: Write it out. Yes. Same.
Paper listens without interrupting.

choices.label: Walk it out
reply: Walk it out. Very efficient.
Feet move, worries shrink.

A:A: You both talk it out. Great teamwork.
Two voices, one solution. {partner} is your sounding board.
Juno and I talk until 4 a.m. Healthy? Mostly.
A:B: You write it out. {partner} talks it out.
Read them your page aloud. They'll love it.
Your notebook and their voice. A team.
A:C: You walk it out. {partner} talks it out.
Walk while they talk. Perfect pairing.
B:A: You talk it out. {partner} writes it out.
Ask them to share a page. Then talk about it.
Words on paper, words out loud. Double processing.
B:B: You both write it out. Lovely.
I can picture it: you and {partner} could swap notebooks and feel less alone.
Journals are therapy with no appointments.
B:C: You walk it out. {partner} writes it out.
Walk to a café. Let them write. You watch the street.
Two coping styles, one cozy afternoon.
C:A: You talk it out. {partner} walks it out.
Walk and talk together. Two birds, one stroll.
Movement helps the words come out anyway.
C:B: You write it out. {partner} walks it out.
Write while they walk. Then swap notes.
Or bring your notebook on the walk. Pause on a bench.
C:C: You both walk it out. Synchronized worrying.
Pretty sure {partner} and you have a 'worry route' around the neighborhood.
Walking side by side. Very healing.

questions.scene: Oswin whispers 'moth,' then looks around, embarrassed.
lines: That's our safe word. Juno's and mine. For arguments. It works. Weirdly well.
questions.question: Mid-argument pause: a silly safe word, or a calm 10-minute break?

choices.label: Silly safe word
reply: A silly safe word. Yes. Mine is 'moth.'
It makes everyone laugh and reset.

choices.label: Calm 10-minute break
reply: A calm break. Very wise.
Fresh air before hard words.

A:A: You both pick a silly safe word.
Choose one with {partner}. Not 'moth.' That's taken.
Laughing mid-argument is underrated.
A:B: Calm break for you. {partner} wants a silly safe word.
Let them say the word. Then take your ten minutes.
Their word, your break. Fair compromise.
B:A: Safe word for you. {partner} prefers a calm break.
Say the safe word, THEN take the break.
Laugh first, breathe second.
B:B: You both pick a calm break.
Ten minutes apart, then back to {partner} with clearer heads.
Mature. Very mature. I'm jealous.

questions.scene: Oswin yawns, then checks whether yawning was rude.
lines: It's late. My brain is loud. Let's make it louder.
questions.question: Late-night mode: deep talks, or silly memes?

choices.label: Deep talks
reply: Deep talks. Oh, I'm in.
The best truths come out at midnight.

choices.label: Silly memes
reply: Silly memes. Perfect.
Laughter heals overthinking.

A:A: You both love deep talks.
Stay up with {partner} and let the big questions bloom.
Like 'what are we?' and 'do fish get thirsty?' Both important.
A:B: Memes for you. {partner} wants deep talks.
Send a meme about existentialism. Both covered.
Then answer their deep question. Just one.
B:A: Deep talks for you. {partner} wants memes.
Start with a meme. Then sneak in a deep question.
Meme to the meaning of life pipeline.
B:B: You both love silly memes.
Send {partner} the worst one you can find. Tonight.
Laughter at 1 a.m. is a love language.

questions.scene: Oswin squints at you, studying your face like it's a puzzle.
lines: Hoo. Okay. I'm a certified overthinker. This is my area.
questions.question: What does your partner overthink the most?
questions.selfQuestion: What do you overthink the most?

choices.label: Texts
reply: Texts. Punctuation panic is real.
'Was that period aggressive?'

choices.label: Plans
reply: Plans. Spreadsheets of feelings.
Plan A, B, C, D.

choices.label: Something they said three days ago
reply: Something from three days ago. That's me.
The replay machine runs all night.

A:A: Texts, and {partner} guessed it.
They know you agonize over every 'ok.' vs 'okay!'
Send them a text without editing. Just once.
A:B: You overthink plans. {partner} guessed texts.
They see you agonize over messages. It's really the calendar.
Plan one thing. Text 'done.' Breathe.
A:C: You replay old conversations. {partner} guessed texts.
They see the typing. They don't see the replay.
Tell them. 'I'm still thinking about Tuesday.' They'll get it.
B:A: You overthink texts. {partner} guessed plans.
They don't see your punctuation spiral. Lucky them.
Tell them about the period panic. They'll laugh.
B:B: Plans, and {partner} guessed it.
They know you have seventeen backup plans.
Let them pick one. Just one. Breathe.
B:C: You replay old conversations. {partner} guessed plans.
They think you're planning. You're reliving.
Ask them about it. They probably don't even remember.
C:A: You overthink texts. {partner} guessed old conversations.
Close. It's the texts about the old conversations.
Send 'no pressure, just overthinking.' It helps.
C:B: You overthink plans. {partner} guessed old conversations.
Your brain is in the future. They think it's in the past.
Plan a cozy debrief. Covers both.
C:C: Something from three days ago, and {partner} knew it.
They've caught you replaying a conversation at 2 a.m.
Tell them. They probably forgot it. In a good way.

questions.scene: Oswin glances out the window at the moon, wide awake.
lines: Insomnia talk. I'm extremely qualified. Sadly.
questions.question: When your partner can't sleep, what do they do?
questions.selfQuestion: When you can't sleep, what do you do?

choices.label: Scroll their phone
reply: Scroll the phone. Blue light buddies.
The glow of regrets and cat videos.

choices.label: Whisper 'are you awake?'
reply: Whisper 'are you awake?' Brave.
Hoping for company at 3 a.m.

A:A: Scrolling, and {partner} knew it.
They've seen the phone glow under the blanket.
Share a cat video. Then both try to sleep.
A:B: You whisper 'are you awake?' {partner} thought you'd scroll.
Surprise! They didn't know you wanted company.
They'll answer next time. Probably groggy. Still sweet.
B:A: You scroll. {partner} thought you'd whisper to them.
They're waiting for your whisper. You're watching reels.
Wake them up once. They'd like the company.
B:B: Whispering 'are you awake?', and {partner} knew it.
They've been woken up many, many times.
They still answer. That's love.

questions.scene: Oswin dips his head shyly when you compliment his feathers.
lines: Compliments make me weird. Please don't give me one right now. Or do. No. Yes.
questions.question: How does your partner react to a compliment?
questions.selfQuestion: How do you react to a compliment?

choices.label: Says 'thank you'
reply: Says thank you. Healthy. Mature.
Accepting kindness is a skill.

choices.label: Deflects with a joke
reply: Deflects with a joke. Relatable.
Humor shield, activated.

A:A: Thank you, and {partner} knew it.
They know you can take a compliment without combusting. Impressive.
Keep accepting love. I'm practicing. I'm at 'thanks, I guess.'
A:B: You deflect with a joke. {partner} expected a 'thank you.'
They're waiting for you to accept it.
Say thank you after the joke. Two-step.
B:A: You say thank you. {partner} expected a joke.
They're ready for comedy. You just accept it.
They'll be so pleased. Accept more often.
B:B: A joke, and {partner} knew it.
They know every compliment gets a punchline.
They still hear the blush behind the joke.

questions.scene: Oswin flaps his wings once, then freezes, as if surprised by his own movement.
lines: Sudden plan changes. I have feelings. Several. In a spreadsheet.
questions.question: If plans suddenly change, how does your partner react?
questions.selfQuestion: If plans suddenly change, how do you react?

choices.label: Rolls with it
reply: Rolls with it. Impressive.
A bendy soul.

choices.label: Needs a minute to recalibrate
reply: Needs a minute. Same.
Brain reboot required.

A:A: Rolling with it, and {partner} knew it.
They know you're the chill one. Unbothered. A rare bird.
Teach me. Slowly. I'll take notes. Then overthink the notes.
A:B: You need a minute. {partner} thought you'd roll with it.
They're already on Plan B. You're still processing Plan A.
Say 'one sec.' It's okay. Really.
B:A: You roll with it. {partner} thought you'd need a minute.
They're tiptoeing around you. You're already on Plan B.
Tell them you're fine. Actually fine. Not owl-fine.
B:B: Needing a minute, and {partner} knew it.
They know to give you a moment before Plan B.
Reboot time is self-care.

questions.scene: Oswin sits very still, then slowly turns to look at you.
lines: Okay, hear me out. A big one. Reassurance.
questions.question: When your partner needs reassurance, what do they do?
questions.selfQuestion: When you need reassurance, what do you do?

choices.label: Asks directly
reply: Asks directly. Brave. Clear.
No guessing games.

choices.label: Drops a tiny hint
reply: Drops a tiny hint. The owl way.
Very subtle. Very me.

A:A: Asking directly, and {partner} knew it.
They know you'll just say 'do you still like me?'
Healthy. Clear. I'm in awe.
A:B: You drop hints. {partner} expected you to ask directly.
They're waiting for words. You're sending signals.
Make the hint bigger. Or just ask. Juno taught me that.
B:A: You ask directly. {partner} expected hints.
They're out here decoding clues. You just say it.
Less detective work for them. They're probably relieved.
B:B: Dropping a hint, and {partner} decoded it.
They know your 'I'm fine' means 'reassure me, please.'
Impressive translation skills.
